item.title: Ukrainian evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky reunite with family
item.description:
The US upped the pressure on its ostensible allies as part of its push for a truce in the Russia-Ukraine war. Kyiv has paused its strikes on Russian refineries at the behest of Washington, which is trying to corral runaway fuel prices, The Wall Street Journal reported, while Reuters said the Pentagon had urged European leaders to calm their rhetoric over the threat of Russian aggression. The moves come as Russia’s foreign minister entered the US to attend a meeting of G20 foreign ministers, and after the Trump administration waived new sanctions on Russian energy and reached a diesel deal with the Kremlin — decisions met with unease in Europe , which sees Washington as unnecessarily pressuring Kyiv. — Prashant Rao

item.title: Iran war live: Tehran eyes 2-day Hormuz plan; Trump says talks ‘going fine’
item.description:
The US oil industry has earned almost $130 billion in profits since the US and Israel began bombing Iran in February. The same companies, according to the New York Times , earned less than $47 billion over the same span of 2025, when oil was comparatively cheap. Shipping and insurance costs have spiked thanks to the war, allowing oil companies to spike their prices. ExxonMobil and Chevron, the nation’s two largest fossil fuel corporations, saw profits surge. According to quarterly earnings reports released on Friday, ExxonMobil’s profits doubled over the same period last year, while Chevron’s grew by 180 percent. BP, another large oil company, reported its profits reached an 18-year high. “I don’t give a damn.” Shareholders are making money. item.description:

According to a report from French newspaper Le Monde , some 320,000 protesters gathered on the outskirts of Paris for a march that was, at the outset, relatively peaceful. Some of the protesters wore Halloween costumes as they marched — and after several weeks of unrest, police were out in force to make sure that things stayed under control. item.title: How Trump and his allies seek to interfere in the US midterm elections
item.description:
People cast their ballots on the first day of early voting for the U.S. midterm elections, in New York, on Oct. 24, 2026. —Ryan Murphy—Getty Images With the midterms approaching, the climate crisis doesn’t seem to be top of mind for most voters. In a recent poll, voters told Gallup that, among 11 issues, the economy, health care, and the war in Iran are the top of their concerns when it comes to this election season. That doesn’t mean climate isn’t on the ballot. The midterms come as the U.S. has faced a slew of climate rollbacks under the first two years of the Trump Administration, including withdrawing from the Paris Agreement , rolling back the landmark endangerment finding , and leasing public lands for oil and gas drilling. item.title: ICE agent charged for hitting Texas immigrant with vehicle during pursuit
item.description:
A Texas grand jury indicted ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales with a charge of second-degree aggravated assault Friday after prosecutors said he deliberately drove his SUV into a fleeing immigrant in early October. Why it matters: This may be the first time an ICE agent has ever been indicted in Texas, making it a rare case of a federal immigration officer facing state charges. What they're saying: Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare announced the grand jury's charge of second-degree aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, namely a motor vehicle. Morales faces two to 20 years if convicted, Teare said. "Just because you have an ICE badge or any badge, if you are in Harris County and you are violating our community members' constitutional rights, there will be repercussions," he said. Catch up quick: Morales struck Miguel Parra Hernandez on Oct. 10 as Parra Hernandez fled on foot.…

item.title: US inmate Christa Pike says she woke up 'confused and in pain' after failed execution
item.description:
Christa Pike, the woman who was convicted of the 1995 torture and killing of her classmate, has broken her silence for the first time since the botched execution attempt in Tennessee last month. In a statement dictated to her lawyers and released on Friday, Pike said she has been in constant pain and doesn’t know why she survived that night. “One month ago on September 30, I walked into the execution chamber at Riverbend men’s prison prepared to die. I had made my peace. Several days later I woke up alone in a hospital confused and in pain,” the statement read. “There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical.
